ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Addiction Psychiatry Consultation — Joe Louis — True-date frame: synthetic events are moved into the patient's historical lifetime. Codes, instruments, and treatments remain modern and are anachronistic.

code.originalText: One-week review, seen the same day by addiction psychiatry: the diagnosis, an antipsychotic, contingency management and cognitive behavioral therapy

text.paragraph: Persecutory thoughts and poor sleep for two months in a 55-year-old man, a retired heavyweight boxer, who uses cocaine most days and collapsed in the street two weeks ago. Please help decide whether this is a cocaine-induced psychosis, a primary psychotic disorder or a neurocognitive disorder, and advise on an antipsychotic, treatment for cocaine use disorder and safety. [S]
Urgency: Within one week, on the same day as his one-week primary care visit. [S]

list.item: Is this a cocaine-induced psychotic disorder, a primary psychotic disorder, or a neurocognitive disorder after a long boxing career?
Should he start an antipsychotic now, which one, and for how long?
What treatment do you advise for his cocaine use disorder, given that no medicine is approved for it?
How should we handle his cardiovascular risk from cocaine and his raised blood pressure?
What harm reduction, safety planning and family involvement do you suggest?

text.paragraph: Mr. Louis, a 55-year-old retired heavyweight boxer and Army veteran, is seen at the request of Dr. Achterberg-Cole one week after intake. He began using cocaine about a year ago at gatherings and then most days, more on trips for paid appearances. About two months ago he became convinced that people were following him and planned to harm him; he has never had such beliefs at other times, and he has no history of psychiatric treatment. He has used no cocaine for ten days. The beliefs are less intense but persist, and he sleeps about four hours. He has had no hallucinations, has not confronted anyone and has no thoughts of harming himself or others. He wants to stop using cocaine and to feel like himself, and he would like to keep his family out of it for now. [S]
Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: Joe Louis was born Joseph Louis Barrow on May 13, 1914, near LaFayette in Chambers County, Alabama, to Munroe and Lillie Barrow, Alabama sharecroppers; he was one of eleven children. [D]
His family moved to Detroit in the summer of 1926, when he was about twelve, and he took up boxing at a local gym there. [D]

He won the world heavyweight championship on June 22, 1937, by knocking out James J. Braddock, defended it about two dozen times (24 or 25 defenses in different sources), and retired as champion in 1949. [D]

He enlisted in the U.S. Army in January 1942 and served through the Second World War, staging 96 exhibition bouts for the troops and donating the purses of two 1942 fights, nearly $100,000, to the Army and Navy relief societies. [D]

Despite large career earnings, he faced a federal tax debt that by 1956 exceeded $1 million in back income tax, penalties and interest; the debt shaped his finances for many years, and the sources describe its resolution differently. [D]

In 1969 he collapsed on a Manhattan street, shortly after a television interview in New York in late June, and was hospitalized for what was described as a physical breakdown; he later said that the collapse resulted from cocaine use. [D]
In the same period he was troubled by fears of a plot against his life, which a reference biography calls paranoid delusions. [D]
He won 68 of his 71 professional bouts, 54 by knockout. [D]

list.item: Cocaine use disorder, severe, with cocaine-induced psychotic disorder (F14.250). Seven DSM-5-TR criteria make a severe cocaine use disorder. The delusions began during heavy use, he has never had psychotic symptoms without cocaine, they are already fading after ten days, and the examination, laboratory tests and MRI show no other cause: this is a cocaine-induced psychotic disorder. A primary psychotic disorder becomes likelier only if symptoms persist beyond about a month without cocaine, and the diagnosis of schizophrenia, which is made too often in Black men, should not be made on a first presentation like this. [S]

Cognition after a long boxing career. A MoCA of 25 after three hours of sleep and during active psychosis does not show a neurocognitive disorder; the MRI is normal. Traumatic encephalopathy syndrome is a research diagnosis under the NINDS consensus criteria, not a clinical one, and chronic traumatic encephalopathy can be confirmed only after death, so neither label belongs in his record. The MoCA should be repeated when he has slept well and been well for some weeks. [S]

Antipsychotic. Symptoms that persist after ten days without cocaine and keep him from sleeping justify an antipsychotic, as the ASAM/AAAP guideline advises. Aripiprazole at a low dose has little effect on weight, glucose, prolactin and the QT interval, which suits a man with raised blood pressure and a borderline lipid profile. Watch for akathisia. After a period of remission, a gradual taper is advised for a stimulant-induced psychosis. [S]

Treatment of cocaine use disorder. No medicine is approved by the FDA for cocaine use disorder. Contingency management is the treatment with the strongest evidence and should be the core of his plan, with cognitive behavioral therapy alongside it. The off-label options in the guideline, such as topiramate or bupropion, can wait while he does well, and the stimulant-based ones (modafinil, or topiramate with extended-release amphetamine) are unsafe after a psychosis and with high blood pressure. [S]

Raised blood pressure and cardiovascular risk (R03.0). Cocaine raises blood pressure and the risk of heart attack, stroke, arrhythmia and aortic dissection. His blood pressure remains raised ten days after his last use, and the ECG shows left ventricular hypertrophy by voltage, so hypertension is likely; it should be confirmed with home readings once he has been without cocaine for some weeks. Beta-blockers are best avoided while he may still use cocaine. [S]

Harm reduction, safety and family. Fentanyl contaminates much of the illicit stimulant supply, and people who do not use opioids have died of it; naloxone and test strips are essential. He has no suicidal or homicidal ideation and no access to firearms, and he is safe to treat as an outpatient with weekly visits. Family can help, but only with his consent and on his terms. [S]

text.paragraph: Data reviewed: Dr. Achterberg-Cole's intake note and safety assessment. Intake ECG (sinus tachycardia, left ventricular hypertrophy by voltage, QTc 436 ms), creatine kinase 262 U/L, blood count, metabolic panel, liver enzymes and hemoglobin A1c 5.5%, all normal. Urine drug test positive for cocaine, negative for fentanyl, other opioids, amphetamines, benzodiazepines and cannabis. TSH 1.9 and vitamin B12 486, normal. HIV, hepatitis C and syphilis negative; hepatitis B not immune. MoCA 25, PHQ-9 8, GAD-7 9, DAST-10 7, AUDIT-C 3. Brain MRI this morning: no contusion, microbleeds or mass; volume normal for age. Fasting lipids today: total cholesterol 204, HDL 44, LDL 128, triglycerides 160 mg/dL. [S]

list.item: Start aripiprazole 5 mg each morning; check weight, blood pressure, akathisia and abnormal movements at each visit, glucose and lipids at four months if still on it, and taper gradually after about six weeks of remission. [S]
Contingency management with twice-weekly urine tests and prize draws for twelve weeks, and weekly cognitive behavioral therapy. [S]
No medicine for cocaine use disorder for now; avoid stimulant-based options. [S]

Home blood pressure readings before the four-week visit; if hypertension is confirmed, a calcium channel blocker or thiazide first, an echocardiogram for left ventricular hypertrophy that also measures the aortic root, and no beta-blocker while he may use cocaine. [S]
Call 911 for chest pain, shortness of breath, weakness, or tearing pain in the chest or back. [S]
Repeat the MoCA once he has been well for some weeks; no traumatic encephalopathy syndrome or chronic traumatic encephalopathy label. [S]
Keep naloxone and fentanyl test strips at home, never use alone, and come back without shame after any use. [S]
Review safety at every visit, with the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline in his phone. [S]
Involve family only if and when he chooses, with a signed release. [S]
Social work for his money worries. [S]

Discussed with Dr. Achterberg-Cole, who saw him the same day. The diagnosis and options were explained to Mr. Louis in plain words; he chose to start aripiprazole and contingency management today. [S]

Follow-up: Dr. Achterberg-Cole continues the visits and prescribing; addiction psychiatry will see him again if psychotic symptoms persist beyond a month without cocaine or return after the taper, if he uses cocaine repeatedly, or if he wants to discuss a medicine. [S]
